title: B2B E-Commerce Platform Selection in APAC: 2026 Buyer Guide
summary: A practical 2026 guide to B2B e-commerce platform selection in APAC — Shopify Plus, Adobe Commerce and SAP Commerce compared with real pricing and a scoring model.
body_markdown:
**Quick Answer:** B2B e-commerce platform selection in APAC should be scored on commercial model fit, integration quality, multi-entity tax handling and three-year TCO — not feature grids. Shopify Plus suits tier-priced distributors, Adobe Commerce fits contract-pricing manufacturers, and SAP Commerce Cloud only justifies its cost with genuine CPQ requirements.


---


Mordor Intelligence values the Asia-Pacific B2B e-commerce market at USD 10.32 billion in 2026, growing at a 22.45% CAGR toward USD 28.41 billion by 2031. That growth number gets quoted in every board deck. What it doesn't tell you is that most of the manufacturers and distributors driving it are running the transaction on a platform that was designed for a US direct-to-consumer brand selling t-shirts.


*Related reading:*[Global E-Commerce Expansion Trends & Operations for 2026: A Step-by-Step APAC Playbook](https://branch8.com/posts/global-e-commerce-expansion-trends-operations-2026-step-by-step-guide)


*Related reading:*[Shopify vs Adobe Commerce Stock Comparison: A 2026 Buyer's View](https://branch8.com/posts/shopify-vs-adobe-commerce-stock-comparison)


*Related reading:*[Global E-Commerce Expansion Trends 2026: An APAC Seller's Data Playbook](https://branch8.com/posts/global-e-commerce-expansion-trends-2026)


That mismatch is the real problem in B2B e-commerce platform selection APAC teams face. It isn't a shortage of platforms — there are dozens. It's that the evaluation criteria most vendors hand you are built around catalogue size, theme flexibility and conversion-rate optimisation, none of which determine whether a Vietnamese factory can quote a Malaysian distributor in MYR with 60-day terms, a tiered price list, and an invoice that satisfies both tax authorities.


*Related reading:*[EU Company APAC Engineering Hub Setup Guide: SG, TW & HK Compared](https://branch8.com/posts/eu-company-apac-engineering-hub-setup-guide)


*Related reading:*[Salesforce Marketing Cloud AI Agents & CDP for APAC Retail](https://branch8.com/posts/salesforce-marketing-cloud-ai-agents-cdp-apac-retail)


This guide starts with the criteria that actually separate winners from expensive rebuilds, gives you real 2026 pricing ranges for Shopify Plus, Adobe Commerce and SAP Commerce Cloud, and closes with a weighted scoring framework you can run internally in a week.


## The nine criteria that decide fit in APAC


Start here, before any demo. If a criterion below scores zero on a platform, no amount of front-end polish recovers it.


### 1. Account hierarchy and buyer permissions


B2B buying is a committee sport. You need company records with multiple locations, multiple buyers per location, and role-based permissions — a purchasing officer who can build a cart but not approve it, a finance controller who can approve up to a limit, a head-office admin who sees every subsidiary's orders.


Shopify's native B2B (company profiles, locations, catalogues) covers two levels cleanly. Adobe Commerce's Company Accounts feature supports deeper hierarchies with requisition lists and purchase-order approval flows. SAP Commerce Cloud models arbitrarily deep organisational units because it inherits from an ERP worldview. Ask specifically: how many levels, and can approval limits differ per currency?


### 2. Price list logic


This is where most APAC deals get complicated. A dealer network typically needs: a base list price, a dealer tier discount, a customer-specific negotiated price, a volume break table, and a promotional override — resolved in a deterministic order, per currency, with an effective date range.


If the platform can only express "price list per customer group," you will end up maintaining thousands of SKU-level overrides in spreadsheets. Ask the vendor to demo price resolution for a single SKU with four overlapping rules and show you which one wins.


### 3. Multi-entity, multi-currency, multi-tax


A Hong Kong holding company selling through Singapore, Taiwan and Australia entities is not a "multi-currency store." It's three legal sellers with different invoice requirements: Singapore GST (9% since January 2024, per IRAS), Australian GST at 10% with ABN validation, Taiwan's Government Uniform Invoice (GUI) numbering, and Hong Kong with no VAT/GST at all. Malaysia's MyInvois e-invoicing mandate has been phasing in through 2024–2026 under LHDN, and Vietnam has required e-invoices since 2022.


The question is not "do you support tax?" It's "which entity issues the document, in which numbering series, and how does it reach the statutory portal?" Usually the answer is a middleware integration, not a platform feature — which is why criterion 6 matters so much.


### 4. Payment terms and credit


B2B in APAC still runs on credit and bank transfer. McKinsey's B2B Pulse research has repeatedly found that B2B buyers are willing to transact large amounts through digital self-serve channels — but only where the commercial terms they already have are honoured online. Practically, you need: net terms per company, credit limit enforcement at checkout, partial payments, and offline settlement reconciliation.


Shopify supports net payment terms on B2B orders natively. Adobe Commerce has payment-on-account. SAP defers to the ERP's credit management. Also check local rails: FPS in Hong Kong, PayNow in Singapore, and virtual-account bank transfer in Indonesia are more common in B2B than card payments.


### 5. Catalogue and product data complexity


Industrial catalogues break naive data models. Configurable products with dependent options, units of measure (each / box / pallet with conversion factors), minimum order quantities, lead times per SKU per warehouse, and technical attribute sets that vary by category. If your SKU count is above roughly 50,000 with heavy attribute variance, that pushes you toward Adobe Commerce or SAP, or toward a separate PIM feeding a lighter storefront.


### 6. Integration surface with ERP and WMS


The platform is rarely the system of record. Stock, price, credit and order status usually live in SAP S/4HANA, Business Central, NetSuite, or a locally hosted ERP that nobody wants to touch. Evaluate the API before the UI: rate limits, bulk operations, webhook reliability, and whether the vendor supports an event-driven pattern or expects polling.


### 7. Regional performance and hosting locality


Latency from a US-East origin to Jakarta or Manila is real. Check the CDN and origin regions available. Shopify runs a global edge network with no region choice. Adobe Commerce on Cloud lets you pick AWS/Azure regions including Singapore, Sydney and Tokyo. SAP Commerce Cloud runs on Azure with regional data centres. If you have data-residency obligations — China's PIPL, Vietnam's Decree 13, Australia's Privacy Act — hosting locality becomes a gating requirement rather than a performance tweak.


### 8. Localisation depth


Traditional Chinese for Hong Kong and Taiwan are not interchangeable with Simplified Chinese. Japanese and Korean need proper text handling in PDFs and emails, not just the storefront. Thai and Vietnamese search tokenisation affects whether your site search finds anything. Ask how many locales the admin supports, not just the storefront.


### 9. Local implementation and support capacity


This is the criterion buyers underweight most and regret first. A platform with three certified partners in your time zone will cost more in delay than a platform with thirty. Check the vendor's regional partner directory and ask for two references in your market and language.


## Pricing in real 2026 numbers


List pricing changes and every enterprise deal is negotiated, so treat these as publicly reported ranges to anchor your budget, then verify with the vendor.


### Shopify Plus


Shopify publishes Plus starting at **USD 2,300 per month on a three-year term, or USD 2,500 per month on a one-year term** . Above roughly USD 800,000 in monthly GMV, pricing shifts to a variable model (commonly cited around 0.40% of GMV, capped at USD 40,000 per month). Payment processing is separate — Shopify Payments rates vary by market, and using a third-party gateway historically attracted an additional transaction fee.


Realistic APAC B2B implementation range for a dealer portal with ERP integration: **USD 60,000–250,000** in build cost, plus apps. Budget USD 500–2,000 per month for the app stack (B2B extensions, tax, ERP connector, search).


### Adobe Commerce


Adobe does not publish list pricing. Reported figures put Adobe Commerce Cloud licences in the **USD 40,000–190,000+ per year** band, tiered on gross merchandise value, with large multi-brand deployments running higher. B2B features (company accounts, requisition lists, quotes) are included in Adobe Commerce B2B, which was folded into the core commerce offering rather than sold separately.


Implementation is the bigger line. A serious APAC B2B build on Adobe Commerce typically lands **USD 150,000–600,000** , and infrastructure/monitoring adds to the licence. Adobe Commerce also carries real maintenance obligations — security patches and version upgrades are not optional, and each major upgrade is a project.


### SAP Commerce Cloud


SAP Commerce Cloud is subscription-priced, negotiated per deal, and generally reported to **start around USD 150,000 per year** and scale well past USD 500,000 for large enterprises. Implementation for a multi-country B2B rollout commonly runs **USD 500,000 to several million** , with 9–18 month timelines.


The honest case for SAP: if you already run SAP S/4HANA and your commerce requirements are genuinely ERP-shaped — complex configure-price-quote, contract pricing, deep organisational hierarchies — the integration savings are real. The honest case against: if you're buying SAP Commerce mainly because you own SAP ERP, you are about to spend enterprise money on requirements a mid-market platform would have covered.


### The regional platforms


SHOPLINE, which originated in Hong Kong and is strong across Greater China and Southeast Asia, prices well below the enterprise tier and carries native support for regional payment methods, WhatsApp and LINE commerce flows, and Traditional Chinese admin. Its B2B feature set is narrower than Adobe's, so it fits distributors with straightforward tier pricing rather than contract-heavy manufacturers. BigCommerce Enterprise typically lands in the USD 1,000–5,000+ per month range with strong native B2B price lists.


### Total cost of ownership over three years


A useful sanity check I run with clients: take licence plus implementation plus 20% of implementation per year for maintenance, plus internal headcount. A Shopify Plus dealer portal often totals USD 250,000–450,000 over three years. Adobe Commerce lands USD 600,000–1.5 million. SAP Commerce Cloud rarely comes in under USD 1.5 million and frequently exceeds USD 3 million. The three-year view is what kills the "licence is cheaper" argument in either direction.

## Why buyers search "Apache" alongside platform selection


One of the more revealing patterns in search data around B2B e-commerce platform selection APAC is how often it collides with Apache Kafka, Apache NiFi and Apache POI. That isn't a typo cluster — it's the same buyer, two weeks later, discovering that the hard part was never the storefront. It was the integration layer.


Here's what those tools actually solve in a B2B commerce architecture.


### Apache Kafka for order and inventory events


Polling an ERP every five minutes for stock levels across 40,000 SKUs and six warehouses does not scale, and it produces oversells. An event-driven pattern publishes inventory and price changes once, and every consumer — storefront, dealer portal, marketplace connector — reads from the same log.


```text
1  # Topic per bounded context, partitioned by SKU for ordering guarantees    2  kafka-topics.sh --create \    3    --bootstrap-server kafka-ap-southeast-1:9092 \    4    --topic inventory.availability.v1 \    5    --partitions 12 --replication-factor 3 \    6    --config retention.ms=604800000 \    7    --config cleanup.policy=compact
```


Log compaction matters here: with a compacted topic keyed on SKU, a new consumer can rebuild current stock state from the log without a separate full-sync endpoint.


### Apache NiFi for the messy file-based flows


APAC B2B still moves a lot of data by SFTP and CSV — dealer price lists, third-party logistics status files, distributor sell-through reports. NiFi is unglamorous and effective for this: watch a directory, validate schema, transform, route failures to a quarantine path, retry. Building the same thing as a cron job plus custom scripts is faster on day one and considerably worse on day 200 when nobody can tell you why Tuesday's file didn't land.


### Apache POI for spreadsheet reality


Your largest distributor will send orders as an Excel file. This will not change because you launched a portal. Apache POI parses those workbooks server-side so a bulk-order upload becomes a first-class channel instead of a manual re-key:


```text
1  try (Workbook wb = WorkbookFactory.create(uploadStream)) {    2      Sheet sheet = wb.getSheetAt(0);    3      for (Row row : sheet) {    4          if (row.getRowNum() == 0) continue; // header    5          String sku = row.getCell(0).getStringCellValue().trim();    6          int qty = (int) row.getCell(1).getNumericCellValue();    7          lines.add(new OrderLine(sku, qty));    8      }    9  }
```


### Pushing it into the commerce platform


On Shopify, the B2B objects are first-class in the GraphQL Admin API, so a company and its buyer can be provisioned programmatically from your ERP's customer master:


```text
1  mutation CreateDealer {    2    companyCreate(input: {    3      company: { name: "Northern Distributors Pte Ltd", externalId: "ERP-40219" }    4      companyLocation: {    5        name: "Singapore HQ"    6        billingAddress: { countryCode: SG, city: "Singapore" }    7        buyerExperienceConfiguration: {    8          paymentTermsTemplateId: "gid://shopify/PaymentTermsTemplate/4"    9          checkoutToDraft: false    10        }    11      }    12    }) {    13      company { id name }    14      userErrors { field message }    15    }    16  }
```


The architectural point: your platform choice should be judged partly on how cleanly it sits behind an integration layer you control. A platform with a complete API and reliable webhooks gives you options later. A platform whose B2B logic is only reachable through its admin UI does not.


## A weighted scoring framework you can run in a week


Don't score platforms on features. Score them on your requirements, weighted by what a failure would cost you. Here's the model I use with manufacturers and distributors — 100 points, adjust the weights to your business and hold them fixed before you see any demos.


### Weights


- **Commercial model fit (20 points)** — price list logic, contract pricing, quotes, MOQ, units of measure
- **Account and approval structure (12 points)** — hierarchy depth, roles, spend limits
- **Integration and API quality (15 points)** — ERP/WMS connectivity, bulk APIs, webhook reliability, rate limits
- **Multi-entity finance and tax (12 points)** — per-entity invoicing, e-invoicing compliance, currency handling
- **Payments and credit (8 points)** — net terms, credit limits, local rails
- **Regional operations (10 points)** — hosting locality, latency, data residency, locale depth
- **Three-year TCO (13 points)** — licence + implementation + maintenance + headcount
- **Partner and support capacity in-region (10 points)** — certified partners in your time zone and language


### Scoring rules


Score each category 0–5, then multiply by weight/5. Two discipline rules make this useful rather than theatrical:


1. **Zero is disqualifying on any category weighted 10 or above.** A platform that cannot issue compliant invoices from three entities doesn't get to win on TCO.
2. **Score from a proof, not a promise.** "On the roadmap" scores 0. Demoed in a sandbox with your data scores 4. Running in a reference customer's production in your region scores 5.


### How it typically resolves


Run honestly, the framework tends to separate three profiles:


- **Distributors with tier-based pricing, under ~50,000 SKUs, 1–3 selling entities.** Shopify Plus usually wins on TCO and speed to launch, and loses points on multi-entity tax and deep hierarchy. Often the right answer anyway.
- **Manufacturers with configurable products, contract pricing, and a dealer network across 4+ markets.** Adobe Commerce usually wins on commercial model fit and hosting locality, and loses on TCO and maintenance burden.
- **Enterprises with SAP S/4HANA, CPQ requirements, and global governance.** SAP Commerce Cloud wins on integration and enterprise controls, and loses badly on TCO and time to value. Verify that the requirements are real before accepting the cost.


The framework's job isn't to pick for you. It's to make the trade-off explicit so the decision survives a CFO review.

## Failure modes worth designing against


A few patterns recur across APAC B2B implementations, regardless of platform.


**Treating the dealer portal as a website project.** The storefront is maybe 30% of the work. Price resolution, credit enforcement, order status sync and document generation are the other 70%, and they're all integration work. Budget accordingly.


**Underestimating data readiness.** In one engagement with a manufacturer selling through a multi-country dealer network, the platform decision was straightforward; getting a single consistent product master and a defensible price hierarchy out of legacy systems was the long pole. If your SKU data lives in three spreadsheets and one ERP with inconsistent units of measure, fix that in parallel or the launch date is fiction.


**Launching everything at once.** Phased rollout by market beats a simultaneous six-country go-live. Start with the market where your commercial terms are simplest, prove the price and credit logic, then replicate.


**Buying for peak complexity.** Gartner has projected that the large majority of B2B sales interactions between suppliers and buyers will occur through digital channels — but "digital" for most distributors means reorder, not configure-to-order. Buying an enterprise platform for a reorder workload is the most expensive mistake in this category.


**Ignoring the offline channel.** Your sales reps will keep taking orders by phone and WhatsApp. Give them an assisted-ordering path in the same system, or you'll be reconciling two order books forever.


## How to evaluate: a five-week sequence


Here's the sequence I'd run if I were making this decision next quarter.


**Week 1 — Write the commercial model down.** Not requirements prose. Actual artefacts: three real price lists with overlapping rules, two real customer hierarchies, one real order that broke your current process, and your entity/tax map by market. This document is your evaluation instrument.


**Week 2 — Fix the weights and shortlist to three.** Use the framework above, set weights before demos, and shortlist by disqualifiers rather than by feature grids. Three platforms is enough; five wastes a month.


**Week 3 — Run a paid proof of concept, not a demo.** Give each vendor or partner the same artefacts from week 1 and ask them to build the price resolution for one SKU family and one company hierarchy in a sandbox. Charge yourself the cost of two weeks of a partner's time; it's the cheapest insurance in the process. Watch how they handle the case that doesn't fit.


**Week 4 — Model three-year TCO with your own numbers.** Licence, implementation, annual maintenance at 20% of build, app/extension subscriptions, hosting, and the internal headcount you'll need to run it. Then add 25% contingency, because integration scope always grows.


**Week 5 — Check references in your region and language.** Two customers in your market, on your platform version, with a comparable integration. Ask what the second year cost, not the first.


Where this is heading: the platform layer is commoditising faster than the integration layer. Shopify keeps absorbing B2B capability that used to justify an Adobe licence; Adobe and SAP keep pushing toward composable, API-first delivery. By 2027 the differentiator in B2B e-commerce platform selection APAC won't be which storefront you licensed — it'll be whether your product, price and credit data is clean enough and event-driven enough to move between storefronts, marketplaces and AI-mediated buying agents without a rebuild. Choose the platform that makes your data portable, and you keep the option to change your mind.
